subject: arcticOutpost
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: arctic research outpost.
Style: Firewatch flat colour.
reasoning:
I'm planning the diorama composition: a snowy base slab with a wooden cabin featuring a pitched roof, glowing windows, and a smoking chimney, plus a radio mast and a Stevenson screen weather station, all rendered in Firewatch's flat warm-gradient style.

Since this is a scenery diorama rather than a creature, I don't need joints -- static props and geometry can live untagged in model space. I'm planning to use flat colors for most surfaces with selective gradients on snow and sky, plus SVG textures for window glow, signage, flags, and gauge faces, backed by a layered mountain silhouette in purple, mauve, and orange to evoke a sunset backdrop.

I'm working out real-world scale: a base disc or irregular slab around 6-6.5m radius, a cabin roughly 4.2m x 3.2m, with layered mountain extrusions set back several meters at increasing heights for depth, while making sure everything sits flush on the ground plane with nothing floating below y=0.

I'm sketching helper functions for parts and extrusions (boxes, lathes, swept tubes for cables/smoke, textured planes for window glows), noting that static geometry without joints just anchors to the root via an `at` position. Then I'm defining the Firewatch-inspired color palette -- warm peach-white for lit snow, lavender for shaded snow, deep purple-blue for the darkest tones.

Now I'm expanding the palette to cabin walls, roof, door, and window glow colors, plus sky gradient tones for distant mountains and dark teal-green trees with snow highlights. I'm thinking through paint techniques, considering a countershade approach for snow or possibly importing a toon/cel shading kit to get that flat, two-tone Firewatch look based on surface normals.

I'll use cel shading with a fixed key light for the walls so different faces get distinct lit/shadow tones, layering flat colors for smaller details, and bump the paint sheet resolution to 2048 for crisper cel edges—keeping in mind texel density drops as more parts get painted onto a shared sheet, so I'm estimating area and texel size to confirm the flat look still reads well at that resolution.

Now I'm sketching the overall layout: base centered at origin facing +Z, cabin offset to the side also facing forward, with the ground sitting at a fixed height. For the base I'm planning a tapered rock/ice form built from an extruded irregular polygon outline in the XZ plane, working out how the outline's local axes map into world space so the shape sits upright and centered correctly.

Still defining the island outline...

For snow drifts, I'm scattering flattened sphere shapes in snowy tones around the cap, letting them sink naturally into the surface. Then I'm placing the cabin off-center on raised stilts above the permafrost, setting its footprint and floor height relative to the ground plane.

Working out the roof geometry now — walls rise to meet the eave line, then a gabled roof with a 30° pitch sits on top, built from extruded triangular end profiles along the ridge axis.

Calculating the slab dimensions for the sloped roof surfaces, factoring in the overhang beyond the walls and the pitch angle to get the correct slope length and box sizing for each roof panel.

So rotating by +a tilts the +Z side down and -a for the -Z side, keeping the slabs matched at the ridge. I'm adding a slightly smaller snow layer on top of each roof slab, shifted along the surface normal and scaled narrower so the roof edge still peeks out at the eave.

Now I'm planning icicles as small downward-pointing cones hanging at the eave, roughly ten of them, plus setting up the cabin's local wall coordinates, floor height, and a wall material that layers horizontal board-seam shading beneath the cel shading.

I'm adding corner trim posts, a teal front door with a cream frame, and a porch deck with steps leading up to it.

Now I'm positioning front-facing windows on either side of the door, planning each as a glowing textured panel with mullion crosses and curtain silhouettes for a warm lit effect.

I realize the glow shouldn't apply to the cream frame itself, so I'll separate the SVG into just the glowing yellow-orange panes with dark mullions, plus an unglowing frame box layered on top. I also want a warm light spill on the snow outside the window, done as a flat trapezoid of solid warm color like the lighting in Firewatch, rather than a soft alpha gradient which would get clipped.

Now I'm placing those trapezoid spills: flat pale-yellow shapes sitting just above the snow surface in front of the windows, avoiding the porch deck area near the door, with one spill for each of the two windows on the front face plus one on each side window.

I'll also add a chimney poking through the roof as a small brick-colored box with a cap, and generate smoke puffs curving upward using a swept path with low-poly icosahedron shapes in soft mauve and white tones that grow in scale as they rise.

I'm positioning the chimney to be embedded in the back slope of the roof, then planning a lattice radio mast tower on the +X side built from four angled legs, roughly 7 meters tall.

Building the tower structure with tapering rods, horizontal rings, X-shaped diagonal braces, and alternating orange-and-cream painted stripes, plus an antenna with a glowing red light on top and guy wires anchoring it to the ground.

Defining the dish's outer shell profile and tilt direction, adding a feed horn and mount, then planning a Stevenson screen weather station box on legs with louvre details.

For the louvres I'll approximate with thin horizontal slat boxes rather than textures. Beside it I'm adding an anemometer mast with rotating cup arms at 120° spacing, a wind vane, a striped snow depth stake, and considering a small gauge plane for a data readout.

I'm weighing whether to pull in the gauge texture from the clockwork kit versus drawing my own SVG thermometer sign to avoid dependency risk, and leaning toward sketching it myself while still relying on the toon kit's cel shading and glow effects, since those seem safe to assume are available.

Now I'm placing the fuel drums beside the cabin at the left side near the origin, working out cylinder dimensions, colors, ring bands, and snow caps to match the Firewatch-style front-left-top lighting.

Next I want crates stacked with wood texture and stenciled "SUPPLY" lettering, then a wooden sled with runners and a strapped tarp bundle leaning near the front, and I'm considering a small tracked snow vehicle as another prop though it may be too complex.

I'll place a simplified blocky snowmobile at front-left instead, with a red-orange nose, black seat, dark teal windshield, track texture, and curved ski shapes, kept to around a dozen parts. Then I'll add a flag pole with a wavy cloth flag near the front center-left using an extruded shape with an SVG texture.

Working out the flag's orientation so it flows toward -X with the wind, then adding a wavy silhouette to the top and bottom edges for a natural flutter. For the pine trees, I'll stack three cone tiers per tree with dark teal-green bases and lighter snow-cap tips, varying sizes via rng and clustering them in a back arc that stays within the cabin's base radius.

I'm adding a few faceted rocks with snow caps for texture, then placing a footprint trail of flattened cylinder decals leading from the door to the fuel drums, offsetting them slightly above the snow surface to avoid z-fighting. For the backdrop, I'm planning jagged mountain layers extruded further back in the scene.

I'm planning a large backdrop rectangle with a vertical gradient from peach horizon to deep rose/purple sky, nesting paint calls for the three-color Firewatch effect. I'm estimating texel density given the backdrop's size versus total painted area, and bumping the paint resolution to 2048 to keep cabin board lines crisp.

Actually, flat colored bands might work better than gradient paint since flat colors don't count against the paint budget -- I could stack four thin horizontal strips to recreate that classic Firewatch sky banding. I'm now sizing the backdrop wall (roughly 20 wide, 12 tall, set back behind the cabin) and weighing whether something this large risks turning into a stage-flat billboard that overwhelms the diorama's actual subject.

I want this to read like a Firewatch-style paper-cutout diorama: layered mountain silhouettes behind a shadow-box frame roughly 14-15 units wide, with the ground base around radius 6. I'll have the backdrop layers rise from floor level (y=0) so they sit naturally behind the base slab rather than floating.

I'm spacing four mountain layers at increasing depth (z from -6.8 nearest to -9.2 farthest, darkest to lightest), with sky bands and a sun placed even further back, checking that none of these intersect the base geometry. For generating the jagged mountain silhouettes themselves, I'll write a ridge function that produces zigzag peak points across the width, starting and ending at ground level.

Snow caps could use a painted threshold based on height plus a zigzag offset for a jagged snowline edge, estimating texture resolution needed for crisp detail across the combined surface area — though I'm also considering skipping the paint approach and just sloping the ridge geometry directly.

Checking the atlas budget: a 2048 paintSize gives roughly 2cm texels across the total surface, which should be sharp enough for board lines around 1.6cm wide, whereas dropping to 1024 would blur at 4cm texels, so 2048 seems like the safer choice.

I'm also thinking about simplifying mountains by splitting into two extrudes for rock and snow-cap polygons, but defining the ridge boundary for snow cover gets complex, so painting a single textured mesh is simpler even though back faces get painted unnecessarily—worth accepting that waste.

For distant layers, I could fake aerial perspective by having the paint gradient itself fade from rock color near the top toward haze/fog color near the base, using vertical UV coordinates to blend the two.

Writing the ridge paint function...

I briefly consider adding light/dark facet shading to peaks like in Firewatch, splitting each ridge into lit and shaded faces using noise or sign-based alternation, but decide to skip that complexity and just keep flat snow coloring, blending toward mist color near the base using a simple mix function.

I'm now checking that the SDK exports everything I need (mix, noise, paint, resolve, rgb, smoothstep, SURFACE) from a single module, then tallying up the total part count across base terrain, backdrop, trees, and cabin to make sure I land within the 180-340 target range.

Continuing the tally for mast, dish, weather station, drums, crates, sled, snowmobile, flag, and footprints — totaling roughly 330 parts, which fits the budget, and I'm estimating the final script will run 600-800 lines. Now I'm listing out the texture definitions I'll need, like window glow, crate stencil, and door sign.

I'll skip the aurora idea but add cloud streak cards — soft pinkish stacked rounded-rect shapes rendered as double-sided cards floating in the sky.

For planes, I'll build textured and flat-colored quads facing specific axes (clouds textured, sun as a flat glowing circle), and plan to clone materials for the glow effect since each textured surface needs its own instance.

Now I'm sketching the mast lights as glowing spheres, then setting up imports for the builder, toon shading kit, and glow kit, pruning any unused ones to avoid typecheck errors. Setting up the base builder config and defining box/vector helper types...

Still writing helper types...

Checking that scale, flat, and rotation options are supported on parts, then working out rod geometry details - using modest polygon sides for the rods to keep triangle count manageable across many instances.

Now I'm setting up the snow paint colors, considering a gradient tint that shifts warmer toward the back using a z-based smoothstep so the snow isn't flat white but picks up subtle peach tones near the sunset side.

For walls, I'm defining a board paint function that creates seams between boards at regular intervals...

Now I'm picking the color palette: cel-shaded walls in red-orange, with the roof in deep teal for complementary contrast against cream trim and yellow lights, following the Firewatch-inspired aesthetic.

Using many cel paints is fine since it's paint count not raw colors, and each painted region just counts toward sheet area. I'm writing a polar coordinate generator function that jitters points around a circle using a seeded random function, then moving on to sketch the outline.

I'm figuring out how to extrude the 2D outline into a star-shaped base polygon in 3D space, then computing scaled radius variations for different layers like ice and snow versions, keeping tree placement radii smaller than the irregular base boundary.

Now I'm layering the cake into strata: a bottom rock layer, a mid ice layer, and a top snow layer, each with increasing radius for a staggered ledge effect, and setting the extrusion thickness and vertical position accordingly.

For the snow drifts, I'm defining a helper that places scaled ellipsoids at various spots around the cake, buried partway into the surface with enough visible height to look like realistic drift bumps.

For the trees, I'm designing them with a trunk cylinder and three tiered cones for the foliage, each topped with a slightly smaller, scaled-up snow cone layered over the apex so it reads as snowfall sitting on the branches above.

Working out the tier dimensions and spacing...

Checking total tree height against the cabin scale -- trees should stay secondary since the cabin is the hero element. Now I'm placing individual trees around a back arc behind the scene, picking x,z coordinates and scale factors so they cluster naturally without overlapping the mast position.

Working out the full layout: cabin centered around x -0.9, z -0.4 with its front face at z 1.2, a porch deck extending forward to about z 2.2 with steps down to z 2.7, and a door offset to x 0.3. I'm moving the chimney to the left side (x -2.2) so it doesn't collide with the mast, which I'm placing at roughly x 3.0, z -0.8 with a small base and guy-wire anchors staked into the ground.

I'm checking that the guy-wire anchor points and the mast itself stay within the circular platform (radius ~5.2), picking anchors like (4.1, -2.6) and (1.8, -2.8) so the wires run clear of the cabin, and considering lowering the mast height slightly to 6.5 for better proportion. I'm also positioning a Stevenson weather station around (3.3, 2.6) and starting to place an anemometer mast, checking each new feature's distance from the platform center stays under the radius limit.

I'm now working on the satellite dish placement, testing a spot near (4.0, 0.4) but finding it too close to the platform edge, so I'm trying a position behind the cabin on the left side instead, adjusting the dish's diameter down to 1.5 and shifting it to roughly (-4.0, -1.2) to keep its total reach within the 5.2 radius limit.

I'm mapping out positions for the fuel drums left-front, keeping them within the safe radius, and figuring out where to put the sled and snowmobile in the front-left area, angling the snowmobile slightly to stay within bounds while leaving room for a firewood stack.

Now I'm placing the firewood stack against the cabin's left wall and sketching footprint paths from the porch steps toward the drums and anemometer, then positioning the flag, Stevenson screen, and anemometer in the front-right cluster so they don't overlap.

I'm reconsidering the flag's placement, settling it on a pole near the cabin's roof ridge, then stacking crates beside the mast on the cabin's right side, checking that the mast legs and crate footprint don't collide, and adding a striped snow stake nearby.

Now I'm placing trees around the back of the scene, checking distances against the mast, guy-wire anchors, and the snow stake so nothing overlaps, adjusting a few tree positions near the edge of the radius to keep spacing reasonable.

Setting up constants for the cabin's position, floor level, wall height, and dimensions, then defining a helper to convert local cabin coordinates to world space before placing the foundation piles.

Still building gable geometry...

I'm working out the slab centreline position, averaging the rafter line's y-value across the span and offsetting it by 0.07 along the surface normal to account for slab thickness.

Now I'm placing the ridge beam box geometry rotated 45° at the roof peak, then adding a snow layer slab offset further along the normal and slid upslope by 0.12 to sit naturally on the pitched surface.

Next I'm adding icicles along the front eave edge as downward-pointing cones, jittered in position along the x-axis, colored icy blue, with their rotation flipped so the tips hang down from the eave line.

Then I'm building the front door: a mustard-colored door box with a cream frame (lintel and side posts), a dark doorknob sphere, a glowing window pane inset in the upper door, and a house number sign plane mounted above it.

Settling on sign centered at 2.1 with size 0.8x0.24, sitting just above the door lintel without much overlap. Now I'm working out the porch deck as a box positioned at floor level, plus two step boxes leading down to roughly ground height, calculating their centers from the floor elevation.

I'll skip adding a porch canopy since it would clash with the main roof's overhang, and instead focus on simple railings along the porch edges using posts and a connecting rail.

I'm also planning a lantern beside the door—a bracket arm with a glowing hanging cylinder shape, cap, and base plus some light spill—then moving on to a reusable window function that builds a frame based on position, orientation, and dimensions.

For the front windows, I'm placing one at lx -1.45 and another at -0.15, each 0.8 wide, so they sit clear of the door's 0.75–1.65 span. I'm skipping shutters since four at 0.35 wide would overlap, keeping just a flower-box detail instead.

Now I'm building out the window box with a snow-capped sill, layering a cream sill box and a slightly smaller snow box on top, then placing the glass pane recessed behind the frame boards so the depth reads correctly. For the end walls, I'm adding matching windows on the +X and -X sides at different heights, with frame orientation flipped to face outward on each side.

I'm drafting a generic `windowAt` helper that takes a center, axis (z or x), sign, dimensions, and texture, mapping local u/v/d coordinates into world space depending on wall orientation, plus a frame-box helper `fb` that swaps dimension order for x-axis walls versus z-axis walls. I'm also considering where to place a small thermometer plaque on the front wall, maybe near the door or under a window.

Now I'm positioning the thermometer plaque on the end wall beside the window (avoiding overlap), sizing it around 0.3x0.9, and sketching out the cab-mounted chimney as a box with dimensions that respect the roof's slope angle so its base sits flush where it meets the roofline and its top extends a bit above the surface.

For the chimney, I'm building a cap box and a darker flue box on top, then working out a brick-pattern paint function that uses mortar lines based on vertical banding plus horizontal offset so the pattern reads correctly whether on an x-facing or z-facing side, combining x+z as the horizontal coordinate since only one varies per face.

Now I'm adding a snow cap on the chimney and planning smoke puffs rising from the top, drifting toward -X to match the wind direction, starting from the computed world position of the chimney top.

Designing smoke puff geometry...

Positioning the log pile against the wall, I decide logs should lie along the z-axis so their circular ends face the viewer, giving a nicer visual of stacked rings rather than side profiles.

For the mast, I'm planning a tapering tower structure with six height levels, legs connecting corner points that narrow as they rise, plus horizontal rods at each level and alternating diagonal braces per face, colored in alternating orange and cream segments.

Totaling parts now: five segments of legs and diagonals plus six levels of horizontals comes to about 64 pieces, with legs thicker than the brace rods. I'm adding a platform at the third level, then topping the mast with an antenna mast extension, cross dipole elements, a glowing red beacon sphere, and a small directional yagi antenna with its own boom and elements.

At the base, I'm considering a concrete footing slab in a dark grey tone, plus a small hazard-striped equipment cabinet near the mast's foot.

I'm placing the cabinet with a textured gauge-panel face for instrument readouts, while reserving the plaque texture for a separate wall sign -- trying to keep the texture set manageable: windows, sign, crate, drum label, gauge panel, tarp pattern, and clouds, using painted stripes instead of a texture for the hazard markings on the stake.

Now I'm working out guy wires running from a point partway up the mast down to small stake anchors, then sizing the legs for the Stevenson screen enclosure.

I'm detailing the Stevenson screen box with painted horizontal slats alternating cream and grey, a slightly tilted roof slab, and considering a touch of snow. Next I'm designing an anemometer on its own pole with a three-armed crosshead and hemisphere cups rotated so their open faces catch the wind properly.

Simpler to just use small closed spheres for the cups since the sides material setting isn't straightforward—stylized but effective. For the vane, I'm thinking of a separate arm rod extending from the pole below the cups.

Rather than a second pole, I'll place the wind vane right at the end of the cabin's roof ridge for a classic look—a short vertical rod with an arrow-shaped body pointing in the direction wind would come from, with tail fins on the opposite side.

Then I'm moving on to the dish assembly: a ground-mounted post with a mounting box and the dish itself.

Still defining dish geometry...

Now I'm checking for spatial conflicts between other objects, like the crate position and porch deck boundaries, to make sure nothing overlaps.

Setting up the flag pole position and dimensions, then working out the flag's wavy outline with a notched swallowtail shape.

The thickness normal computes out to the z-axis, so the flag's face is in the x-y plane, visible from the front viewer side. For the snowmobile at its position with a 20° yaw rotation, I'm setting up a helper function that transforms local coordinates into world space using standard rotation formulas for x and z.

I need to be careful about Euler rotation order since combining yaw with pitch (for tilted parts like the windshield or skis) in a single rotation vector would apply rotations in the wrong local frame — so I should keep yaw-only parts simple and handle pitched components separately to avoid incorrect orientation.

For combined pitch and yaw, I'll build a quaternion using a "YXZ" Euler order so yaw applies before local pitch, wrapping this in a helper function that takes pitch, yaw, and roll angles and returns the correct quaternion — I'll use this `quat` option generally for these parts.

Now I'm laying out the snowmobile itself: a dark track box with specific dimensions and position, then starting on the wheels or cylinders at both ends of the track.

Continuing with the geometry, I'm adding rotated cylinders for the track ends, an orange rear body box, a teal-black seat, rack slats, a tapering frustum-shaped hood/nose in orange, and a tilted teal windshield positioned toward the front.

Now I'm placing handlebars and grips across the top, then working out the ski geometry with upturned tips, figuring out the correct rotation direction so the tip end angles upward.

I still need to add headlight glow, ski struts connecting to the body, and a cargo bag, keeping the part count near 14. Then I'm positioning a separate sled nearby, checking its distance and orientation so it doesn't collide with the snowmobile, adjusting its placement and yaw so the length sits safely within range.

Writing sled geometry...

Still placing load geometry... now I'm adding stanchions, side rails, and a tarp-covered bundle with rope straps, then positioning textured crates on top of the trailer bed.

For the drums I'm planning cylinders with rim rings and a lid disc, plus a flattened sphere snow cap on one. Since texturing the cylinder's curved surface directly would distort any label, I'm opting to add a small flat plane decal offset slightly in front of the curved surface instead.

I'm also laying out footprint positions as a series of points forming an arc from the porch steps toward the snowmobile and drums.

Since the sled path conflicts, I'll redirect it toward the weather station instead, heading past the anemometer toward the Stevenson screen with about 9 steps along a catmull curve. For the footprint visuals, I'm using small flattened oval cylinders offset left and right to represent alternating steps, rotated to match the heading angle computed from the path tangent.

Now I'm figuring out the yaw rotation so the footprint's elongated axis aligns with the direction of travel, and setting its color to a deep shade that reads against the snow. I'm also working out light-spill trapezoids cast on the snow from windows, extruding a trapezoidal outline along the ground plane to approximate where window glow would fall, positioning them near the window locations on the house.

I'm checking that two adjacent spills (each about 1.1 wide, centers 1.3 apart) overlap slightly, which would cause z-fighting since they're coplanar, so I'll offset their heights slightly or merge them into a single polygon. I'm also verifying the spills don't collide with the sled or drum props nearby, and double-checking the snow cap's top surface height after extrusion to make sure footprints and spills sit correctly above it.

I'm skipping the door lantern's porch spill for now, then moving on to designing the sky backdrop as a series of horizontal color bands mimicking a Firewatch-style sunset gradient, from warm orange-yellow at the horizon up through pink and purple tones toward the top, each band spanning a set vertical range and full width.

I briefly consider curving the backdrop into an arc of segments for a wraparound effect, but decide the extra complexity isn't worth it since the camera is likely front-facing, so I'll keep the bands flat.

Now I'm placing the sun as a glowing circle with a softer halo ring behind it, positioning it in the sky layer so it sits just behind the far ridge, letting its upper portion peek above the terrain.

For clouds, I'm planning thin pink streak shapes as rounded rectangles layered above the mountains to suggest soft horizontal cloud bands.

Writing ridge generation logic...

Writing paint logic for ridge coloring...

I'll simplify to just two rock tones below the snow line and two snow tones above, avoiding uniform diagonal banding across the whole silhouette.

Now designing the texture assets: a gauge face with cream dial and red needle, a sign reading "ARCTIC STATION 7" on a cream board in bold serif, and a window texture with a warm yellow-orange gradient, dark cross mullions, and a teal curtain on one side.

I'm adding a small plant silhouette on the windowsill for one window variant, keeping the second window simpler with just shelves. The glow effect should apply uniformly across the whole texture including the dark mullions, since emissive dark is still valid.

Now I'm thinking through the builder API constraints — parts without bones default to model space under the untagged root, static models can skip joints entirely, and glow only works on MeshStandardMaterial parts, not flat-painted cel parts. I'm also noting the lathe helper takes an outline of typed coordinate pairs along with axis, segment count, and color options.

Writing scene setup and palette...

Cabin wall offsets don't matter here. For the cel shading, when the surface isn't lit enough the shadowed tone applies to whichever base color is chosen, including seam colors. Now I'm defining more paint colors like a cream tone...

Defining jittered blob shapes and extrusion slabs...

Checking shading confirms the top face is lit while sides facing away from the light stay shadowed, and the base sits flush at ground level. Now I'm placing snow drift positions around the periphery—scattering a handful near the sled, cabin edges, and open areas with varying sizes, making sure none overlap the cabin or crate placements.

I'm also scattering a few rocks near the scene edges, checking each coordinate against existing tree positions to avoid overlap.

Now I'm ready to start writing the actual build function, setting up the builder, rng seed, and the cabin structure.

Defining helper functions for parts...

Writing window gradient SVG texture...

Now I'm designing the second window (lamp with warm shelf glow), a station sign with cream background and bold "STATION 7" text plus coordinate lines, and a wooden crate texture with plank lines and a bordered frame.

Still drafting more assets... a fuel drum label with a flame icon, a teal gauge panel with a cream dial and red needle, an ochre tarp with diagonal stripes and patches, and starting on a clouds texture.

Now I'm moving to the cabin construction itself, setting up coordinate constants for cabin position, floor height, and dimensions, then defining a helper to map local cabin coordinates into world space. I'm placing the foundation piles as small cylinders sunk into the ground at the corner and midpoint positions before working on the floor beams.

Adding walls, corner posts, trim bands...

Computing the roof slope angle and panel centers, I'm working out the eave overhang and deriving the slab centerline position by tracking how the roof line height drops with horizontal distance from the ridge.

Adding the snow slab box...

I'm checking whether the snow slabs actually reach the ridge line or fall short, working through the offset distances given the slope angle and slab length to see if there's a gap at the peak.

Then I'm positioning the eave edge and icicle cones, computing the vertical and depth offsets so the icicles sit right at the roof's outer corner under the overhang.

Next I'm working out the barge boards at the gable ends, placing cream-colored boxes along the roof edges sized to match the slab extension, then moving on to the chimney and door placement before circling back to correct the porch deck's front wall coordinate relative to the building depth.

I'm positioning the porch deck panel and the two steps leading down from it, computing their world coordinates by offsetting from the center and floor level, then considering whether to add plank lines for detail before deciding to skip that and just paint the boards.

I'm sketching the railing layout with posts at each side corner, top and mid rails connecting them, then moving to the door design with a mustard-colored panel, darker inset panel details, and a small glowing window plane.

For the door I'm adding frame sides, a top header, a sphere knob, and skipping the door spill effect. Then I'm designing a wall-mounted lantern with an arm rod extending from the wall to a lantern body made of a cone cap and a glowing cylindrical housing.

Now I'm laying out window positions around the cabin: two on the front wall, one on the east end, and one on the west end near the firewood stack, each with their own offsets and orientation. I'm starting to write a reusable function to generate window geometry from these parameters.

Writing window frame geometry...

Adjusting snow ledge placement...

The glass pane uses a plane geometry facing the correct direction with the texture applied, confirming colored textures override part color. Now I'm moving to the chimney, smoke, and weather vane details, defining brick and mortar coloring, then setting up the mast's position and height dimensions.

Building the mast lattice geometry...

Adding the top antenna with crossbars and a beacon sphere, then mounting a simple Yagi antenna with boom and decreasing-length elements off the side of the mast, plus a joining mount rod.

Now I'm routing three guy wires from a level-4 corner down to ground anchors in different directions, each anchored by a small steel box at ground level, with the wires rendered in plum-colored thin rods -- checking that one wire path doesn't collide with the crates below.

I'm also verifying that the Stevenson screen's roof height and footprint don't intersect the wire running from near the mast base to the second anchor point, confirming the vertical and horizontal gaps clear.

For the instrument cabinet, I'm placing it near the mast base away from the crates, checking that the wire path clears its footprint at ground level, and sketching it as a small box with a sloped roof and a gauge-plane texture on its front face.

Now I'm adding ground cables running from the cabinet to the mast base using sagging catmull-rom sweeps, plus a second cable rising from a higher mast point down to the cabin's roof eave for added realism.

I need to check the cable path against the roof overhang so it doesn't clip through geometry, adjusting the sag curve so it passes just under the eave before reaching the wall insulator. I'll add a small insulator cylinder at the wall attachment point, and then the dish, flag, and weather elements are already complete.

Snow details can be kept minimal: flat snow boxes on crate and drum tops, skipping porch railing snow and footprints. Now I'm ready to assemble the full build script, being careful with type annotations around color parameters and the sweep/catmull curve helpers for the cable geometry.

Writing ridge generation logic...

Verifying the step count divides evenly so the ridge closes properly at the edges, then I'm defining color layers for each ridge depth, giving nearer hills deeper purple-blue tones and distant ones lighter orange-pink hues like the Firewatch art style, with each layer having its own peak position and height range.

I'm also computing snow-line thresholds relative to each ridge's max height, and placing the sun off-center behind the hills to establish directional lighting for the shading.

Setting band widths and depths for the sky layers, then picking two alternating dark teal-green tones for the pine silhouettes to match that Firewatch-style palette. Still finalizing details like extrude thickness and vector conversions before writing the final scene code.

Writing dish geometry code...

Continuing the dish mount cylinder, hub, and base geometry, then orienting the dish toward the sky direction and sketching out the Stevenson screen weather station with its legs and slatted body box.

Now I'm detailing the roof slab with a slight roll rotation, adding a snow layer on top, then placing the anemometer pole and head cylinders.

Adding anemometer arms...

Now I'm positioning the weather vane on the ridge of the roof, with a pole, arrow shaft and cone head pointing one direction and a tail fin pointing the other, plus cardinal direction rods.

I still need a flag stake with painted stripes, a snow lump on the drums, and I'm working out footprint paths so they don't collide with the anemometer or stake positions, adjusting coordinates to keep everything clear.

For the footprint geometry I'm using thin scaled cylinders tinted slightly darker than the ground to look flattened into the snow. Now I'm pulling everything together into the final code, double-checking TypeScript parameter annotations and making sure all the helper imports I need are actually included.
